summary: Build check: utils.js loads cleanly via vm.runInContext; no syntax errors, no runtime exceptions.
AC-1 (eviction at 200): Verified via 20+ assertions. Cap holds precisely — inserting entry 201 evicts the oldest. Bulk insertion of 1000 entries correctly retains only entries 801–1000.
AC-2 (_size() accuracy): Returns 0 on fresh cache, increments correctly per insertion, holds at 200 after overflow.

AC-3 (set/get behavior preserved): Stored names are retrievable; missing keys fall back to slug portion; falsy names (empty, whitespace) are rejected; trimming is applied; get(null) returns null without throwing.
AC-4 (no duplicate order-tracker entries): Duplicate set() calls for the same key update the value but leave _keys length unchanged. Verified stable under 100 repeated updates to the same key.
Regression: All 93 test files, 2851 tests pass — zero regressions.

Edge-case stress (37 assertions): FIFO eviction order confirmed; key-update does not re-order insertion position (consistent with implementation intent); falsy/null/undefined key inputs handled safely; exact boundary cycling (200 cap, 10-step add/evict loop) correct.

comments.note: Update-does-not-reorder behavior (FIFO, not LRU): when set() is called on an existing key, the value is updated but the key retains its original insertion position in _keys. This means a frequently-updated entry will be evicted at the same point in sequence as when it was first inserted. This is consistent with the FIFO design and works correctly for the 200-entry cap, but differs from LRU semantics. If usage patterns shift so that project names are constantly refreshed for the same keys, the eviction order will not adapt — worth documenting in a future code comment.

summary: Code review PASS. The bounded ProjectNameCache implementation is clean, correct, and architecturally sound.
Reviewed utils.js lines 52–109 (the IIFE and its public API) against all four acceptance criteria and the four Review Dimensions.

Maintainability: Excellent. The IIFE closure cleanly encapsulates _cache and _keys. The hasOwnProperty guard uses the safe Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call() form, avoiding potential prototype-chain collisions. All three public methods (set, get, _size) are clearly documented with JSDoc. The _size() method is appropriately flagged as testing-only.

Best Practices: Fully consistent with the project's vanilla-JS convention (var throughout, no ES6+, no bundler dependencies). The eviction logic correctly keeps _keys and _cache in sync — shift+delete is atomic within the synchronous JS event model, so no torn-state risk. The hasOwnProperty check before push ensures _keys never holds duplicate entries.

Performance: O(1) get and O(1) amortized set (shift() is O(n) on the _keys array, but at MAX_SIZE=200 this is negligible — ~200 element moves maximum, effectively constant for this use case). No concerns at the stated cap.

Future Context: The FIFO-not-LRU eviction semantics are appropriate for project display names (low churn, user navigates a bounded set of projects). The implementation is a well-scoped, self-contained fix that does not introduce technical debt. The WP-004 handoff note correctly flags that the same file will be modified by the makeProjectCacheKey WP — no conflict risk since the changes are in logically independent regions.
Fix-Forward applied: Added a FIFO-vs-LRU clarifying comment inside set() (non-behavioral — no logic change). This addresses the QA observation about documenting eviction semantics.

comments.note: Added a 4-line FIFO-vs-LRU comment inside set() (lines 70–73) clarifying that updating an existing key refreshes its value but does not reposition it in the eviction queue. This is non-behavioral — no logic was changed. Addresses the QA observation about undocumented eviction semantics.

The _keys array's shift() is O(n) for eviction. At MAX_SIZE=200 this is negligible (~200 element moves worst-case). If the cap is ever raised significantly (e.g., 10,000+), consider switching _keys to a doubly-linked list or using a Map, which provides O(1) ordered iteration and O(1) delete.
